newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian profits to add 0.8 pts to Q4 GDP.
newsitem.headline: Australian profits to add 0.8 pts to Q4 GDP.

text.p: Profits earned by large companies would contribute about 0.8 percentage points to December quarter growth in nominal GDP, economists said on Thursday.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics heavily revised up its earlier estimates of company profits.

The data showed September quarter seasonally adjusted profits were revised up by A$535 million, the June quarter rose by A$384 million, the March quarter by A$512 million, December 1995 by A$427 million and September 1995 by A$408 million.
Earlier quarters were little changed.
The revisions meant that year-to growth rates for the quarters from September 1995 to June 1996 would rise.
The bureau said the revisions stemmed from late responses and corrections from surveyed companies.
"Seasonal factors have also been re-analysed," the bureau said.
The 0.8-percentage-point contribution to growth is only that implied by large companies surveyed in Thursday's release.
GDP measures are based on the much wider concept "gross operating surplus", which includes small companies, unincorporated businesses and other profit-earning operations.
In the September quarter the remainder of gross operating surplus contributed 0.4 percentage points to GDP growth in trend terms.
Assuming that trend movement were repeated in the December quarter, then total GOS would contribute 1.1 percentage points to quarterly GDP growth (after rounding).
Before the company profits data was issued, economists had expected a small positive contribution from gross operating surplus, typically 0.1 percentage points.
Accordingly, GDP forecasts were now likely to be revised up.
The following table gives economists' average December quarter forecasts expressed as contributions to quarterly GDP growth and updated with today's data.
Items marked with an asterisk are now backed, at least partially, by published data.
The analysis excludes minor items and GDP-P, which is difficult to forecast.
